## How to use this notebook

This is where you work out the questions for the **3. Public Spending** page (`R/page_spending.R`) before they go on the website.

1. **Pick a question** for each figure. Ideas: `docs/question_bank.md`. Variables: `docs/variables.md`.
2. **Work it out** in the figure's chunk below: numbers first, then a quick chart.
3. **Write the finding** under **Title** (one sentence that states the result) and **Caption** (2-3 sentences: what the chart shows, the key number, what it means). Say "is linked to", never "causes".
4. **Copy it into the page file**: the `title`, the `caption`, and your ggplot code as `plot = function(d) { ... }` (see `R/page_story.R`).

**Shared functions** (from `analysis/_setup.R`):

| Function | Gives |
|---|---|
| `summarise_question(data, "x", "y")` | Spearman r, r at similar income levels (beyond GDP), r within each income group |
| `spearman(data, "x", "y")` | n, r, p-value |
| `beyond(data, "x", "y")` | r after removing the effect of GDP per capita |
| `by_income(data, "x", "y")` | r within each income group |
| `quick_scatter(data, "x", "y", log_x = FALSE, log_y = FALSE)` | a quick exploratory scatter, to look at the data (draw the website's chart yourself with ggplot) |

Add, remove or rename the Q sections freely.

## Q1: Is it inequality before or after taxes and transfers that matters?

The chart code is the same as `redistribution_chart()` in `R/page_spending.R`; **if you change the chart, change it in both places.**

**Variables:** `swiid_gini_mkt` (Gini before taxes and transfers), `swiid_gini` (after), their difference (`redistribution`, Gini points removed) and `under5_mort` (log scale), 2010s averages.

```{r q1-chart}
# Figure 1: inequality before vs after taxes and transfers ---------------------
# The same countries twice: left panel with the Gini BEFORE taxes and transfers
# (market income), right panel AFTER (disposable income). The difference
# between the two is how much the state redistributes.
# d: 2010s data, one row per country (given by the template).
redistribution_chart <- function(d) {
  colours <- c("Low income" = "#86b6ef", "Lower middle income" = "#3987e5",
               "Upper middle income" = "#1c5cab", "High income" = "#0d366b")

  d <- d %>%
    filter(!is.na(swiid_gini_mkt), !is.na(swiid_gini), !is.na(under5_mort), !is.na(income)) %>%
    mutate(redistribution = swiid_gini_mkt - swiid_gini) %>%
    # Long format: one row per country per Gini measure, so facet_wrap can
    # draw the two measures as two panels
    tidyr::pivot_longer(c(swiid_gini_mkt, swiid_gini), names_to = "measure", values_to = "gini") %>%
    mutate(
      measure = factor(measure, levels = c("swiid_gini_mkt", "swiid_gini"),
                       labels = c("Before taxes and transfers", "After taxes and transfers")),
      tip = paste0("<b>", country, "</b>",
                   "<br>", income,
                   "<br>Gini ", tolower(measure), ": ", round(gini, 1),
                   "<br>Taxes and transfers remove ", round(redistribution, 1), " Gini points",
                   "<br>Under-5 mortality: ", round(under5_mort, 1), " per 1,000")
    )

  ggplot(d, aes(x = gini, y = under5_mort)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
                colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.8) +
    suppressWarnings(geom_point(aes(colour = income, text = tip),
                                size = 2, alpha = 0.8)) +
    facet_wrap(~ measure) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colours, name = NULL) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    labs(x = "Gini index (SWIID, 0-100)", y = "Under-5 mortality (log scale)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
}
```

```{r q1, fig.width = 9}
d <- d %>% mutate(redistribution = swiid_gini_mkt - swiid_gini)
summarise_question(d, "swiid_gini_mkt", "under5_mort")[1:2]
summarise_question(d, "swiid_gini", "under5_mort")[1:2]
summarise_question(d, "redistribution", "under5_mort")[1:2]
redistribution_chart(d)
```

**Title:** What matters is inequality after taxes and transfers, not before

**Caption:** Preliminary: inequality before taxes and transfers is barely linked to child mortality (r = -0.19; 0.11 at similar income levels). Inequality after them is strongly linked (r = 0.60; 0.52 at similar income). Countries where taxes and transfers remove more inequality have fewer child deaths, even at similar income (r = -0.40). ## Q2: Are countries whose governments spend more less unequal?

Jacob's question (`PublicSpendingVsIncomeInequality.Rmd`). The chart code is the same as `spending_inequality_chart()` in `R/page_spending.R`; **if you change the chart, change it in both places.** Uses 2010s averages: in 2022 alone only 72 countries have both values, against 143 here.

**Variables:** `gov_expense` (or `edc_spending`, % of GDP) and `swiid_gini`, 2010s averages.

```{r q2-chart}
spending_inequality_chart <- function(d, education = FALSE) {
  colours <- c("Low income" = "#86b6ef", "Lower middle income" = "#3987e5",
               "Upper middle income" = "#1c5cab", "High income" = "#0d366b")
  x_var   <- if (education) "edc_spending" else "gov_expense"
  x_label <- if (education) "Education spending (% of GDP)" else "Government expense (% of GDP)"

  d <- d %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[x_var]]), !is.na(swiid_gini), !is.na(income)) %>%
    mutate(tip = paste0("<b>", country, "</b>",
                        "<br>", income,
                        "<br>", x_label, ": ", round(.data[[x_var]], 1),
                        "<br>Gini (SWIID): ", round(swiid_gini, 1)))

  ggplot(d, aes(x = .data[[x_var]], y = swiid_gini)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
                colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.8) +
    suppressWarnings(geom_point(aes(colour = income, text = tip),
                                size = 2.3, alpha = 0.85)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colours, name = NULL) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = "Gini index (SWIID, after taxes and transfers)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```

```{r q2}
summarise_question(d, "gov_expense", "swiid_gini")[1:2]
summarise_question(d, "edc_spending", "swiid_gini")[1:2]
spending_inequality_chart(d)
spending_inequality_chart(d, education = TRUE)
```

**Title:** Countries whose governments spend more are less unequal

**Caption:** Preliminary: where government spending is a bigger share of the economy, inequality is lower (r = -0.49, 143 countries; -0.33 at similar income levels). Education spending alone shows almost no link (r = -0.17; -0.06 at similar income). TODO
